language_wrapper: You have {length_n} balls arranged in a row, colored using {total_colors} distinct colors labeled 1 through {total_colors}. For each color i (1 ≤ i ≤ {total_colors}), you must use exactly the number of balls specified by the vector {counts_list}, listed in order of color labels i = 1, 2, ..., {total_colors}. Adjacency is restricted by the unordered forbidden-pair set {forbidden_pairs}: if (u, v) appears in this set, then colors u and v may not be adjacent in either order; in particular, (i, i) forbids two i-colored balls from being consecutive. How many valid arrangements satisfy all the exact-count and adjacency constraints?
hardness_rationale: The seed problem counts sequences over three colors with a single local constraint (no two greens adjacent) and no fixed totals per color, allowing a simple stars-and-bars style placement count. Our family adds: (1) an exact count vector for each color, forcing global constraints and eliminating unconstrained multiplicities; and (2) a general forbidden-adjacency set across colors (including self-adjacency blocks), requiring a transfer-matrix or high-dimensional dynamic programming argument rather than simple placements. These enhancements create intricate dependency across positions and colors, introduce nontrivial edge cases (e.g., interactions between cross-color blocks and self-blocks), and demand more advanced combinatorial techniques.
notes: Proof sketch of correctness: Let colors be 1..c with exact counts k_i and a symmetric adjacency-forbidden set F (unordered pairs). Build an allowed matrix A with A[i][j] = 1 iff (i+1, j+1) not in F. Consider the recursive bijection between valid sequences and the DP described in the verifier: states are (last_color, remaining_counts), where remaining_counts records how many balls of each color remain to be placed. From any state, choosing next color x is permitted iff remaining_counts[x] > 0 and either no last_color exists yet or A[last_color][x] = 1. Each transition reduces remaining_counts[x] by one and updates last_color = x. The base case corresponds to placing all balls (sum remaining_counts = 0), yielding exactly one sequence. This DP enumerates each valid sequence exactly once (by position-wise construction) and disallows any invalid adjacency by the A constraint, ensuring correctness. Uniqueness follows from the deterministic decrement of the remaining counts by the chosen next color. Hence the DP computes precisely the number of valid arrangements. Advanced solution approaches mirror transfer-matrix methods for constrained words with fixed letter counts, or inclusion–exclusion on adjacency violations, both consistent with the DP result.
source_question: Take out 17 balls from an ample supply of red, green, and blue balls (these balls are completely identical except for their colors) and arrange them in a row. It is required that no two green balls are adjacent. Find the number of arrangements that meet the requirements.
